Short answer: There is no credible evidence that the Rothschild family created the U.S. Federal Reserve or that they control the global financial system. Reliable historical records and central‑bank documentation show the opposite.

What the evidence shows
- Why and how the Fed was created: The Federal Reserve was established in response to repeated U.S. financial panics (especially 1907). Key steps included the Aldrich‑Vreeland Act (1908), the National Monetary Commission’s work, the 1910 Jekyll Island discussions among U.S. bankers and officials, and the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 passed by Congress and signed by President Woodrow Wilson. The participants and sponsors documented in archives were American policymakers and bankers (e.g., Nelson Aldrich, A. Piatt Andrew, Paul Warburg of Kuhn, Loeb & Co., Henry P. Davison of J.P. Morgan, Frank Vanderlip of National City Bank). There is no documented role for the Rothschild family in designing or passing the Federal Reserve Act.
- Who controls the Fed: The Federal Reserve System is a public institution with a unique public‑private structure. The Board of Governors in Washington is a federal agency; its members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Monetary policy is set by the FOMC, where Board members hold the majority. The Fed is accountable to Congress and remits its net earnings to the U.S. Treasury.
- Global financial system: No single family or private group “controls” it. It is a decentralized network of national central banks, regulators, commercial banks, markets, and international bodies. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), for example, is owned by member central banks (public authorities), not private families. Oversight and policy are distributed across countries and institutions.
- The Rothschilds today: Rothschild & Co is a respected advisory and wealth‑management firm, but it is far smaller than the world’s largest banks and does not control central banks or the global financial system.

Why the myth persists
- Secrecy around the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting and the historic prominence of several banking families has fueled speculation. But primary sources and official histories identify the actual participants and legislative path; they do not support claims of Rothschild control.

Short answer: It’s not accurate that China currently has more retirees than workers. However, China is aging rapidly, and the share of retirees is rising fast relative to the working-age population.

What the numbers show today
- Working-age people still outnumber retirees. In 2023, about 61% of China’s population was of working age (commonly measured as 16–59 or 15–64), while around 21% were aged 60+ (about 15% were 65+). The old‑age dependency ratio (65+ relative to 15–64) was roughly 22–24% in 2022–2023—well below 100% (which would mean more retirees than workers). Sources: China’s National Bureau of Statistics; World Bank; UN World Population Prospects.

Why China is moving toward a much older population
- Very low fertility for a long time: Fertility has been well below the replacement level of 2.1 for years, around 1.0–1.2 in recent years, despite policy shifts from the one‑child policy to two‑ and then three‑child policies. Economic pressures (housing, education, childcare costs), later marriage and childbearing, and urbanization all depress births. Sources: UN World Population Prospects; NBS birth data.
- Longer life expectancy: Big gains in longevity over the past four decades mean more people are living into older ages. Source: World Bank.
- Large cohorts now retiring: Earlier baby‑boom cohorts are entering retirement while much smaller cohorts follow into the labor force, shrinking the worker‑to‑retiree ratio.
- Low statutory retirement ages: China’s current retirement ages (generally 60 for men; 55 for many female white‑collar workers; 50 for many female blue‑collar workers) are low by international standards, which increases the number of retirees at any given time. Authorities have said they will gradually raise the retirement age, but the starting point is low. Source: Official statements reported by Xinhua.

Where the trend is headed
- UN projections indicate China’s 65+ share will approach about 30% by 2050, and the old‑age dependency ratio could roughly double to around 50–60% by mid‑century. That would mean roughly one retiree for every two workers—still not “more retired than working,” but much tighter than today. Source: UN World Population Prospects 2022 (medium variant).

Key sources
- National Bureau of Statistics of China (age structure, births/deaths): http://www.stats.gov.cn
- UN World Population Prospects 2022 (fertility, projections): https://population.un.org/wpp/
- World Bank (old‑age dependency ratio, life expectancy): https://data.worldbank.org
- Xinhua, on plans to gradually raise retirement age: https://english.news.cn/

Short answer: Pieces that claim mRNA COVID‑19 vaccines are broadly harmful typically rely on errors that contradict large, high‑quality bodies of evidence. Common problems and what the best evidence shows:

- Calling mRNA vaccines “gene therapy”
  • Error: Suggests vaccine mRNA alters your DNA.  
  • What we know: Vaccine mRNA stays in the cell cytoplasm, does not enter the nucleus, does not integrate into the genome, and degrades within days. This is foundational molecular biology and is confirmed in non‑clinical and regulatory reviews.  
  • Sources: CDC; EMA Comirnaty assessment; Pardi et al., Nature Rev Drug Discov 2018.

- Misusing passive safety databases (e.g., VAERS) as proof of causation
  • Error: Treats raw reports as verified vaccine injuries or deaths.  
  • What we know: VAERS is an early‑warning system; reports are unverified and cannot establish causation without medical review and follow‑up studies. Large linked‑record studies have not found increased non‑COVID mortality after vaccination.  
  • Sources: VAERS data guide (CDC/FDA); MMWR: Non–COVID mortality risk lower in vaccinated populations (Vaccine Safety Datalink).

- Overstating myocarditis risk while omitting context
  • Error: Highlights post‑vaccine myocarditis but ignores absolute risk, clinical course, and the higher myocarditis risk from SARS‑CoV‑2 infection itself in most groups.  
  • What we know: Myocarditis after mRNA vaccines is rare, concentrated in young males after dose 2, generally mild/short hospital stays, and risk‑benefit strongly favors vaccination for prevention of severe COVID‑19.  
  • Sources: CDC; Patone et al., Nature Medicine (large self‑controlled case series).

- Misrepresenting biodistribution or “spike toxicity”
  • Error: Claims vaccine components or spike protein “spread throughout the body” and persist at harmful levels.  
  • What we know: Non‑clinical studies show lipid nanoparticles and mRNA concentrate at the injection site and draining lymph nodes with transient, low‑level distribution elsewhere; spike or mRNA are detectable in blood only briefly at low levels. No credible evidence of harmful persistence in humans.  
  • Sources: EMA Comirnaty non‑clinical review; Ogata et al., Clin Infect Dis 2022 (transient antigenemia).

- Ignoring large effectiveness and safety datasets
  • Error: Cherry‑picks small, low‑quality, or in‑vitro studies while overlooking population‑level evidence.  
  • What we know: Vaccination substantially reduced severe disease and deaths; modeling estimates millions of lives saved in 2021 alone. Updated vaccines continue to protect against hospitalization, with waning for infection but durable protection against severe outcomes.  
  • Sources: Watson et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2022; multiple CDC/vision-network MMWRs.

- Incorrect claims about fertility, pregnancy, and miscarriage
  • Error: Asserts impaired fertility or elevated miscarriage without high‑quality support.  
  • What we know: Large cohort and registry studies show no reduction in fertility and miscarriage rates within expected background ranges; temporary, small changes in menstrual cycle length have been observed and resolve.  
  • Sources: Shimabukuro et al., NEJM 2021 (pregnancy registry); Wesselink et al., Am J Epidemiol 2022 (fertility); Edelman et al., Obstet Gynecol 2022 (menstrual cycles).

- Confusing correlation with causation in excess‑mortality discussions
  • Error: Attributing excess deaths to vaccination without adjusting for age, infection waves, and baseline risk.  
  • What we know: Vaccinated people have equal or lower non‑COVID mortality than comparable unvaccinated people; most excess mortality tracks infection waves and healthcare strain, not vaccination.  
  • Sources: MMWR (Vaccine Safety Datalink non‑COVID mortality); national statistics agencies and peer‑reviewed analyses.

How to vet claims in any review:
- Check whether it’s a systematic review following PRISMA with transparent methods, predefined inclusion criteria, and risk‑of‑bias assessments. Narrative reviews that lack this often cherry‑pick.
- See whether claims align with large, independent datasets (national registries, randomized trials, CDC/EMA/FDA safety monitoring) rather than isolated lab or case reports.
- Beware of treating safety‑signal hypotheses as established facts without confirmatory studies.

Short answer: Congress does not prohibit the NIH from researching the causes of mass shootings.

What exists is an appropriations rider—commonly called the Dickey Amendment—that since 1996 has said federal health funds may not be used to “advocate or promote gun control.” It was first applied to CDC (1996) and later extended to NIH and other HHS agencies (2012). While this language led to a years‑long chilling effect on federally funded gun‑violence research, it does not ban research itself. Federal guidance in 2013 clarified that research is permitted, and since FY2020 Congress has explicitly funded firearm‑injury and mortality prevention research at both CDC and NIH (e.g., $25 million annually split between the two agencies), which can include studies relevant to mass shootings.

Why the rider exists: It was adopted amid concern in the mid‑1990s that federally funded research was being used to advocate for gun‑control policies. The rider’s intent was to bar advocacy with federal funds—not to forbid scientific research.

Sources:
- Public Law 104‑208 (1996) (the “Dickey Amendment” language: funds may not be used to “advocate or promote gun control”)
- Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2012, applying similar language across HHS, including NIH (Pub. L. 112‑74)
- Presidential Memorandum (Jan. 16, 2013): clarifies that the Dickey language does not prohibit research on gun violence (Federal Register/White House archives)
- Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020 (Pub. L. 116‑94): first dedicated federal funding in decades for firearm‑injury research at CDC and NIH; see NIH and CDC announcements on firearm‑injury research funding

Short answer
- Heusinger was not “Hitler’s chief of staff.” During World War II he served as a senior staff officer in the Army High Command (OKH), heading its Operations Division and, for a brief period in July 1944, acting as Chief of the General Staff of the Army after Kurt Zeitzler resigned. He was wounded in the 20 July 1944 bomb attack at Hitler’s headquarters and was later detained and released without charges.
- After the war, Allied investigators did not charge him with war crimes. In the 1950s, as West Germany rearmed within NATO during the Cold War, he was brought back for his staff expertise. He became the first Inspector General of the Bundeswehr (1957–1961) and then served as Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee (1961–1964)—the alliance’s senior military officer—reflecting NATO’s policy of integrating West Germany and using experienced, vetted professionals.

Why this happened (context)
- Postwar vetting: Heusinger was held and questioned but not indicted at Nuremberg; he was released in 1947. There is no evidence he was convicted of war crimes.
- Cold War priorities: NATO and the Adenauer government prioritized rapid, credible rearmament against the Soviet Union. That meant recruiting experienced former Wehrmacht officers who were cleared by denazification and Allied screening.
- Professional reputation: Heusinger was a career staff officer specializing in operations and planning, which made him valuable for building the new Bundeswehr and later for alliance-level coordination at NATO.

Clarification on titles
- He was briefly acting Chief of the General Staff of the German Army (OKH) in July 1944, not Hitler’s personal chief of staff.
- At NATO he was Chairman of the Military Committee (1961–1964), not “chief of staff for NATO forces” (the operational commander is SACEUR; the Chairman is the alliance’s senior military advisor).

- NATO, “Former Chairmen of the Military Committee – General Adolf Heusinger (1961–1964)” (official NATO biography and dates).

- Herbert Hoover (1929–1933): The Great Depression began months into his term. Following the 1929 market crash, a cascade of banking panics, monetary contraction, deflation, collapsing output, and a global trade slump drove unemployment to about 25% by 1933 and slashed employment. The downturn ran essentially through the end of his presidency, leaving far fewer jobs than when he took office. (Federal Reserve History; BLS historical estimates; NBER dates)

- Donald Trump (2017–2021): After three years of job growth, the COVID‑19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented, sudden employment collapse in March–April 2020 (about 22 million payroll jobs lost in two months). Substantial but incomplete recovery followed, so by January 2021 total nonfarm payrolls were still below January 2017 levels, making him the first president since Hoover to leave with fewer jobs than he started with. - The standard benchmark is BLS total nonfarm payroll employment (seasonally adjusted), comparing the month a president takes office to the month he leaves. Hoover predates that series, but the well‑documented collapse in employment during 1929–1933 leaves no reasonable doubt that jobs were lower at the end of his term.

Short answer: There’s good evidence Hitler suffered long‑standing gastrointestinal complaints—including severe flatulence—but no single, proven underlying disease. The best‑supported explanations are a functional bowel disorder (IBS‑like), compounded by his diet and by the many drugs he was given.

What is well documented
- His personal physician, Theodor Morell, repeatedly noted “meteorism” (bloating/flatulence), abdominal cramps, and constipation, and treated him with anti‑gas and antispasmodic remedies (for example charcoal tablets, belladonna/atropine derivatives), bacterial preparations such as Mutaflor (E. coli Nissle 1917), and cycles of laxatives and other drugs. These notes are cited and analyzed by medical historians.
- Reputable biographers (e.g., Ian Kershaw) and medical studies (e.g., Fritz Redlich, MD) describe chronic gastrointestinal symptoms from the 1930s onward.

Most likely reasons (no definitive diagnosis)
- Functional GI disorder: Medical assessments of the surviving records conclude his pattern fits a functional bowel disorder (IBS‑like) rather than a specific structural disease.
- Diet: Hitler adhered to a meat‑free diet and reportedly ate large amounts of vegetables and pastries; such diets can increase intestinal gas in susceptible people. Definitive food intolerances (e.g., lactose) are unproven.
- Medications and stress: Morell’s drug regimens (anticholinergics like belladonna/atropine, laxatives, occasional opioids and stimulants at times) can slow or disrupt gut motility, promoting constipation, bloating, and gas. High stress and anxiety also exacerbate functional GI symptoms.

Bottom line
- He did have frequent flatulence, but it’s best explained as part of chronic, functional gastrointestinal trouble aggravated by diet and medications—not a single, clearly identifiable organic disease.

Sources for further verification
- Fritz Redlich, Hitler: Diagnosis of a Destructive Prophet (Princeton University Press, 1998) – medical analysis based on primary medical records.
- Leonard and Renate Heston, The Medical Casebook of Adolf Hitler (1979) – synthesis of Morell’s notes and other documentation.
- Ian Kershaw, Hitler: 1889–1936 Hubris (1998) and Hitler: 1936–1945 Nemesis (2000) – biographical accounts noting long‑standing digestive complaints.

Short answer: Because Kiribati’s islands lie on both sides of the Equator (north and south) and on both sides of the 180th meridian/International Date Line (east and west). That geographic spread puts parts of the country in the Northern, Southern, Eastern, and Western Hemispheres.

Key points
- Kiribati consists of widely scattered island groups (Gilbert, Phoenix, and Line Islands) that straddle the Equator and the 180th meridian/International Date Line. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica; CIA World Factbook.

- You’ll often see Kiribati described as the only country with land in all four hemispheres because its own territory crosses both the Equator and the 180th meridian. Some countries with far‑flung overseas territories could also be argued to have land in all four hemispheres, but Kiribati’s core territory alone achieves this.

Short answer: The International Court of Justice did not rule on 26 January 2024 that Israel is committing genocide. It found that South Africa’s genocide allegations are “plausible,” that there is a serious risk of irreparable harm to protected Palestinian groups in Gaza, and it ordered Israel to take provisional measures under the Genocide Convention while the case proceeds. The Court has not decided whether genocide is occurring; that merits question will be decided later.

What the ICJ actually decided on 26 Jan 2024
- Asserted prima facie jurisdiction over South Africa v. Israel under the Genocide Convention.
- Found that at least some of the rights asserted (for Palestinians in Gaza to be protected from acts under Article II of the Convention) are plausible and at risk of irreparable prejudice.
- Ordered provisional measures requiring Israel to:
  - Prevent acts prohibited by Article II of the Genocide Convention (including killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction in whole or in part).
  - Ensure its military does not commit such acts.
  - Prevent and punish direct and public incitement to commit genocide.
  - Enable the provision of urgently needed basic services and humanitarian assistance.
  - Preserve evidence related to alleged genocidal acts.
  - Report to the Court within one month on steps taken.
- The Court expressly stated it was not at that stage determining whether genocide is being committed.
- It also condemned the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas and called for the immediate release of hostages.

Why the Court issued these measures
- On the limited record at the provisional-measures stage, the Court considered:
  - The scale of death, injury, destruction, and displacement of Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023, and the severe deprivation of essentials (food, water, medicine, shelter), as documented by UN bodies, indicating a real and imminent risk of irreparable harm to protected rights under the Convention.
  - Certain statements by senior Israeli officials that, in the Court’s view, could be interpreted as dehumanizing or as calling for actions potentially prohibited by the Convention, raising concerns about possible genocidal intent or incitement that warranted urgent precautionary measures.
- These factors met the legal threshold for “plausibility” of rights under the Convention and for urgent provisional measures to prevent irreparable harm pending a full merits judgment.

Reliable sources
- ICJ, Order on Provisional Measures, 26 Jan 2024: “Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip (South Africa v. Israel)” (official order and reasoning)
  https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/192/192-20240126-ord-01-00-en.pdf
- ICJ Press Release summarizing the order (26 Jan 2024)
  https://www.icj-cij.org/press-releases
- UN OCHA situation updates on Gaza humanitarian conditions (context the Court referenced)
  https://www.unocha.org/occupied-palestinian-territory
- Reuters and BBC summaries consistent with the above:
  - Reuters explainer (Jan. 26, 2024): https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/what-did-world-court-order-israel-do-gaza-2024-01-26/
  - BBC News report (Jan. 26, 2024): https://www.bbc.com/news/world-67673437

Bottom line: The ICJ did not rule that Israel is committing genocide on 26 January 2024. It ordered precautionary measures because genocide allegations were deemed plausible and there was a serious risk of irreparable harm, pending a final decision on the merits.

Short answer: There’s no credible evidence that New York Gov. Kathy Hochul “wants quarantine camps” or wants to imprison people merely suspected of having a disease. That claim stems from mischaracterizations of two different items—one defunct bill and one health‑department rule—neither of which created “camps,” and neither amounts to criminal imprisonment.

What actually happened

- A416 (a past bill that never became law): An Assembly bill introduced years before Hochul became governor would have allowed health officials, during a declared health emergency, to seek detention of people who were proven to be contagious. It never passed, never reached a vote, and was withdrawn in January 2022. Independent fact‑checkers have repeatedly found claims about “quarantine camps” from this bill to be false. Sources: Associated Press fact check; PolitiFact; New York State Assembly bill history.

- 2022 DOH isolation/quarantine regulation (10 NYCRR 2.13): New York’s Department of Health adopted a rule during COVID-19 that allowed civil isolation or quarantine orders for people who were cases, contacts, or suspected cases of serious communicable diseases—typically at home or another appropriate location. It did not establish “camps,” and it was not a criminal law. Critics argued it allowed overly broad executive power; in July 2022 a trial‑level state court struck the rule down, finding the agency exceeded its authority and raising due‑process concerns. Later, an appellate court dismissed the lawsuit on standing grounds (a procedural issue), not on the merits. Sources: Borrello v. Hochul (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2022) decision; subsequent appellate filings/coverage; Reuters and AP fact checks summarizing the rule.

Key points

- Isolation and quarantine are long‑standing public‑health tools used by states nationwide for serious infectious diseases. They are civil health orders, not criminal punishment or “imprisonment,” and are often carried out at home.

- Neither the withdrawn bill nor the DOH regulation created “quarantine camps,” and there is no credible evidence Hochul advocated for such camps.

Sources you can check
- Associated Press, “New York isn’t setting up COVID quarantine camps” (debunks A416 claims)
- PolitiFact and Reuters fact checks on “quarantine camps” claims in New York
- Text/history of A416 on the New York State Assembly website
- Borrello v. Hochul (trial court decision, July 2022) invalidating 10 NYCRR 2.13; subsequent appellate docket and coverage noting dismissal on standing grounds
- New York Codes, Rules and Regulations (10 NYCRR 2.13) describing isolation and quarantine procedures

Bottom line: The “quarantine camps”/imprisonment claim is a false or grossly misleading characterization of New York public‑health measures.

Short answer: The premise isn’t quite right. By nominal dollars, the national debt rose more under President Obama (about $9.3 trillion) than under President Trump (about $7.8 trillion). As a share of the economy, the biggest run‑ups occurred during World War II. However, Trump did preside over the largest single‑term increase in nominal dollars. Sources: U.S. Treasury “Debt to the Penny”; Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB); Washington Post Fact Checker.

Why debt rose so much during Trump’s term:
- Pre‑pandemic tax cuts reduced revenue. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) was estimated by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) to increase federal deficits by roughly $1.5 trillion over 2018–2027 before interest (about $1.9 trillion including interest). Source: CBO (Dec. 2017, April 2018 updates).
- Higher discretionary spending. Bipartisan budget deals in 2018 and 2019 raised defense and non‑defense spending caps, adding hundreds of billions to deficits over the following decade. Sources: CBO cost estimates; CRFB summaries.
- COVID‑19 emergency response. In 2020, Congress and the Trump administration enacted large relief packages—the CARES Act (~$2.2T), Families First (~$190B), PPP and Health Care Enhancement (~$480B), and the December 2020 Consolidated Appropriations Act (~$900B). - Very restrictive access to the main weapons used in school shootings:
  - Handguns: near‑total prohibition on private ownership in Great Britain via the Firearms (Amendment) Act 1997 and Firearms (Amendment) (No. 2) Act 1997; extensive licensing remains only for limited categories (Northern Ireland has a different regime but still stringent licensing).   - Semiautomatic center‑fire rifles were already banned after Hungerford (1988). Source: Firearms (Amendment) Act 1988.

- Low gun prevalence: Civilian firearm ownership in the UK is among the lowest in high‑income countries (roughly 5 guns per 100 residents, versus ~120 per 100 in the US). Low prevalence reduces offender access and opportunities. Source: Small Arms Survey 2018 (Karp).
- Low firearm violence overall: Firearm homicide in England & Wales is a small fraction of all homicides and remains low by international standards, further reducing the base rate of gun attacks, including at schools. Source: ONS, Homicide in England and Wales; Offences involving firearms.
- Evidence on access and mass shootings: While the UK’s specific school‑shooting outcome is hard to ascribe to one law, international evidence shows that making high‑capacity/handgun access more difficult is associated with reductions in mass shootings and firearm deaths (e.g., Australia after 1996; systematic reviews of firearm laws). The broad, well‑documented pattern is no fatal school shootings post‑Dunblane.

Bottom line: The UK’s post‑1996 regime—especially the effective removal of handguns from general civilian circulation, stringent licensing, low gun prevalence, and active police oversight—has made gun attacks at schools extremely difficult, and none have resulted in fatalities since Dunblane. - Cycle timing: Large cohort studies using app-tracked cycles found a small average increase in cycle length (about 0.5–1 day) after vaccination, with a return to baseline within one or two cycles. A larger shift was seen mainly in the uncommon situation of two doses in the same cycle, which also resolved quickly (Edelman et al., Obstet Gynecol 2022; Edelman et al., BMJ Medicine 2022).
- Flow/bleeding: Some people reported temporarily heavier or earlier bleeding; survey data suggest this is usually short‑lived (Lee et al., Science Advances 2022; RCOG guidance 2023).

Why this can happen (biologic plausibility)
- Immune–reproductive crosstalk: Vaccination activates the immune system. Immune signaling can transiently affect the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis (which sets cycle timing) and the endometrium (which is partly regulated by immune cells), leading to a one‑off shift in ovulation or shedding (Male, BMJ 2021; RCOG 2023).
- Short‑term stressors: Fever, systemic inflammation, and stress around vaccination can also nudge cycle timing by a few days. These are temporary processes.

Why fertility is not harmed
- Time to pregnancy: A large prospective study of couples trying to conceive found no reduction in fecundability (the probability of conceiving each cycle) after COVID‑19 vaccination in either partner. By contrast, recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection in the male partner was linked to a short‑term decrease in fecundability—supporting vaccination as the safer option (Wesselink et al., Am J Epidemiol 2022).
- Assisted reproduction: Studies from IVF programs report no differences in ovarian stimulation response, egg/embryo quality, implantation, or clinical pregnancy rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients (summarized by ACOG/ASRM; see ACOG 2024).
- Professional and public‑health consensus: CDC, WHO, ACOG, and RCOG all state that COVID‑19 vaccines do not cause infertility. These conclusions are based on clinical trials, post‑authorization surveillance, and multiple cohort studies.

When to seek care
- If menstrual changes persist for more than a few cycles, are very heavy, or are accompanied by other concerning symptoms, consult a clinician to rule out other causes (e.g., thyroid issues, fibroids, PCOS), since vaccination‑related changes should be short‑term.

Short answer: Because federal law makes evacuation assistance for private U.S. citizens a reimbursable service. The promissory note is the legal instrument that records the debt so the government can recover the transportation costs after getting people out quickly in a crisis.

- Statutory requirement: Under the State Department’s Basic Authorities Act, the Secretary of State may evacuate U.S. citizens when necessary, but must do so on a reimbursable basis and obtain an agreement to repay from evacuees (22 U.S.C. § 2671(b)(2)). - Policy purpose: This protects taxpayer funds and complies with appropriations law (avoiding gifts of public funds). It lets the government move people rapidly without collecting payment on the spot, then bill them later for the transportation provided.
- Longstanding practice: The reimbursement requirement has existed for decades (codified in the 1956 Basic Authorities Act and retained through subsequent amendments). The Department’s public guidance consistently tells travelers they must sign a promissory note and will be billed if they take a U.S. government evacuation transport.

What is well documented:

- What labs report: Under federal guidance issued during the pandemic (pursuant to the CARES Act), laboratories were required to report COVID‑19 test results and certain demographic details to state/local public health authorities for surveillance. Those authorities could then share standardized line‑level data with CDC under data use agreements. This is routine public health reporting, not the creation of a national human DNA database.
  Sources: HHS COVID‑19 Laboratory Data Reporting Guidance (June 4, 2020); 45 CFR 164.512(b) (HIPAA public health disclosures)

- What PCR tests do (and don’t do): Diagnostic PCR tests for COVID‑19 are designed to detect SARS‑CoV‑2 genetic material in a patient specimen. They are not designed to sequence or catalog a person’s human DNA. While a swab can contain human cells, using human genomic material for other purposes would require separate protocols, authorizations, and ethical/IRB oversight; it is not part of standard diagnostic testing.
  Source: U.S. FDA, COVID‑19 Testing Basics

- What CDC received and used: CDC aggregates case and testing data for surveillance, typically with limited identifiers or de‑identified data for national statistics, dashboards, and research. CDC and partners also conducted genomic surveillance by sequencing SARS‑CoV‑2 viral genomes from residual diagnostic specimens to track variants—this targets the virus, not human genomes.
  Sources: CDC, Genomic Surveillance for SARS‑CoV‑2; CDC, COVID‑19 Case Surveillance (public use data documentation)

Given the above, there is no credible evidence that CDC amassed “the largest collection of human data in history” via PCR tests. The available evidence supports standard public health surveillance of test results and viral genomes, conducted under existing legal and privacy frameworks.

Short answer: Because many of the strongest, most-cited findings in early education come from small, intensive, targeted programs for disadvantaged children—not from large, universal systems. When those results (including very large “returns on investment”) are presented as if they will reliably occur under universal pre‑K at scale, the claim goes beyond what the broader evidence supports.

What the research actually shows
- Large returns come from targeted, high‑intensity programs:
  - James Heckman’s well‑known ROI estimates (often quoted in policy debates) are based on programs like Perry Preschool and Abecedarian—small, expensive, and targeted to highly disadvantaged children—not universal systems. Those studies find big, lasting gains and high returns, but they are not directly generalizable to broad universal programs serving all children.
    - Sources: Heckman et al., Journal of Public Economics (2010); Heckman et al., NBER (2016).
- Universal/statewide pre‑K results are mixed and highly quality‑dependent:
  - Tennessee’s statewide pre‑K (a randomized study) showed early test‑score gains that faded and turned negative on several middle‑school outcomes, underscoring that scaling without consistently high quality can disappoint.
    - Source: Lipsey, Farran, Durkin, American Educational Research Journal (2022).
  - Boston’s universal pre‑K (lottery-based study) found short‑run test‑score fadeout but positive longer‑run outcomes in high‑school graduation, SAT‑taking, and reduced disciplinary incidents—suggesting high‑quality urban programs can deliver meaningful benefits.
    - Source: Gray‑Lobe, Pathak, Walters, NBER Working Paper 28756 (2021).
  - Tulsa’s universal pre‑K has shown a mix of positive results, with benefits often larger for disadvantaged students and more modest for others, again pointing to heterogeneity by population and program quality.
    - Source: Gormley and colleagues; see Bartik et al., Upjohn Institute working papers (various years).
- Targeting vs. universality matters for average impacts:
  - Because disadvantaged children tend to benefit most, universal programs (which serve many non‑disadvantaged children) usually show smaller average effects than targeted programs. Reviews from mainstream policy researchers emphasize that program design and quality control determine whether universal pre‑K achieves strong, durable gains.
    - Source: Cascio & Schanzenbach, The Hamilton Project (Brookings), 2013.

Bottom line
- It is accurate that high‑quality early education can produce important benefits—especially for disadvantaged children—and some universal programs (e.g., Boston, Tulsa) show encouraging longer‑run outcomes when quality is high.
- It stretches the evidence to imply that universal pre‑K, as commonly implemented at scale, will consistently yield the very large long‑run gains or ROI observed in boutique, targeted programs. The more careful claim is that impacts at universal scale depend heavily on program quality, dosage, and the populations served.

References
- Heckman, J. et al. The Rate of Return to the High/Scope Perry Preschool Program. Journal of Public Economics, 2010.
- Heckman, J. et al. The Lifecycle Benefits of an Influential Early Childhood Program. NBER Working Paper, 2016.
- Lipsey, M., Farran, D., Durkin, K. Effects of a Statewide Pre-Kindergarten Program on Children’s Achievement and Behavior through Sixth Grade. American Educational Research Journal, 2022.
- Gray‑Lobe, G., Pathak, P., Walters, C. The Long‑Term Effects of Universal Preschool in Boston. NBER Working Paper 28756, 2021.
- Cascio, E., Schanzenbach, D. The Impacts of Expanding Access to High‑Quality Preschool Education. The Hamilton Project (Brookings), 2013.
- Bartik, T. et al. Tulsa universal pre‑K studies. W.E. Upjohn Institute working papers and related peer‑reviewed articles.

Short answer: In April 1975, Biden opposed President Ford’s request because he believed further U.S. military aid to South Vietnam would be futile and he did not want an open‑ended, executive‑driven evacuation of large numbers of South Vietnamese without explicit congressional authorization. He said he would support funds to evacuate Americans, but not to restart or prolong the war, and he initially resisted tying U.S. evacuation money to evacuating Vietnamese civilians. Within weeks, however, he voted to fund and admit Indochinese refugees once Congress set the policy and appropriations.

Details (with sources):
- Military aid: Ford asked Congress for emergency military assistance to prop up South Vietnam. Biden opposed any renewed military aid, arguing the war was lost and additional aid would not change the outcome; he would support funds to get Americans out but not to continue fighting (Associated Press, Aug. 18, 2021; Washington Post Fact Checker, Aug. 19, 2021).
- Evacuating Vietnamese civilians: In an April 14, 1975 meeting with Ford and Senate Foreign Relations Committee members, according to a declassified memorandum, Biden said the United States had “no obligation, moral or otherwise, to evacuate foreign nationals other than diplomats,” and he didn’t want evacuation funds for Americans “mixed” with evacuating Vietnamese. He and other lawmakers also objected to large‑scale admissions without clear congressional approval (Gerald R. Ford Presidential Library, Memorandum of Conversation, April 14, 1975; Washington Post Fact Checker, Aug. 19, 2021; AP, Aug. 18, 2021).
- Later vote for refugees: After Ford sent a specific plan and Congress took up refugee legislation, Biden voted for the Indochina Migration and Refugee Assistance Act (Public Law 94‑23, May 1975), which funded the admission and resettlement of up to 130,000 refugees (AP, Aug. 18, 2021; congressional records summarized by the Washington Post Fact Checker, Aug. 19, 2021).

Short answer: Wisconsin sits at the intersection of ideal natural conditions for cranberries and a mature industry cluster, so it can grow a lot of fruit efficiently and reliably.

Key reasons, with sources:
- Soils and geology: Central and northern Wisconsin have extensive glacial sand and peat deposits with naturally low pH and excellent drainage—exactly what cranberries require. Sand is also readily available for the routine “sanding” practice that invigorates vines and suppresses pests. Sources: UW–Madison Division of Extension (cranberry production resources); USDA NRCS Plant Guide for Vaccinium macrocarpon.
- Water availability and management: Cranberry beds are engineered (not natural bogs) with on‑farm reservoirs and reuse systems. Wisconsin’s abundant surface and groundwater let growers flood for frost protection, pest control, and harvest, then recirculate water—critical for both yield and fruit quality. Source: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, “Cranberry agriculture and water.”
- Climate fit: Cool nights, a relatively long, temperate growing season, and reliably cold winters provide the dormancy, bloom conditions, and fall color development cranberries need. Sources: UW–Madison Extension; USDA NRCS.
- Scale, infrastructure, and research: Wisconsin has by far the most cranberry acreage in the U.S., plus nearby processing capacity, storage, and a strong grower network. Ongoing research and extension support (UW–Madison and USDA‑ARS) have improved cultivars and management, raising yields and consistency. Sources: USDA NASS; UW–Madison/USDA‑ARS cranberry programs.
- The result shows up in the data: In recent years Wisconsin typically produces about 55–65% of U.S. cranberries. For example, USDA’s Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts Summary reports Wisconsin at roughly 60% of national output in multiple recent seasons. Source: USDA NASS, Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts Summary (most recent editions).

Short answer: Because China became the world’s dominant manufacturing and final‑assembly hub at the same time the United States was running large current‑account deficits and U.S. firms and retailers shifted sourcing to China after trade barriers fell. Those forces made U.S. goods imports from China surge far faster than U.S. exports to China.

Key drivers (with high-confidence evidence):
- WTO entry and PNTR removed trade uncertainty. Congress granted China permanent normal trade relations in 2000 and China joined the WTO in 2001, locking in low U.S. tariffs and encouraging offshoring and long‑term supply contracts. Empirical work shows PNTR/WTO substantially increased U.S. imports from China (and exposure of U.S. industries to Chinese competition). Sources: Pierce & Schott (AER 2016); Autor, Dorn & Hanson (JEP 2016); CRS.
- China’s rapid industrialization and export‑oriented manufacturing. China scaled up modern manufacturing, logistics, and infrastructure, becoming a low‑cost, high‑scale producer. Its share of world merchandise exports rose from ~3% in 1995 to ~13–14% by the mid‑2010s. Sources: WTO statistical reviews; World Bank.
- Global value chains concentrated final assembly in China. Multinationals reorganized production so that parts from many countries are assembled in China. U.S. trade statistics count gross value, so the bilateral deficit records the full value of assembled imports even when much of the value added originates elsewhere. OECD TiVA shows a large foreign value‑added share in China’s exports in the 2000s (around one‑third then, declining as domestic content rose). Sources: OECD TiVA; Hummels–Ishii–Yi (vertical specialization).
- U.S. saving shortfall vs. China’s excess saving. By accounting identity, the U.S. current‑account deficit reflects that the U.S. invests more than it saves; China has run persistent surpluses. This macro gap “allocates” a large bilateral deficit to China given its role in manufacturing. Sources: Federal Reserve (Bernanke’s “global saving glut”); IMF External Sector Reports.
- Price and policy competitiveness. China maintained a tightly managed (and widely assessed as undervalued) currency during the mid‑2000s and provided export‑supportive policies (e.g., VAT rebates), boosting price competitiveness; the renminbi appreciated later and the assessment of undervaluation diminished. Sources: IMF External Sector Reports; Peterson Institute analyses.
- U.S. demand and retail sourcing. Strong U.S. consumer demand for low‑priced goods, plus big‑box retail and e‑commerce sourcing strategies, amplified the shift to Chinese suppliers once trade barriers and logistics frictions fell. Sources: CRS; WTO/World Bank documentation on trade costs and logistics.

Clarifications:
- The ~$400 billion figure refers to the bilateral goods deficit at its peak (about $419 billion in 2018). The U.S. runs a services surplus with China, which partially offsets the goods gap, but the overall bilateral balance has still been heavily negative. Sources: U.S. Census Bureau; BEA.
- Since 2018, tariffs and supply‑chain diversification have reduced the bilateral goods deficit from its peak, but the structural drivers above explain the long run rise from the 1990s to the late 2010s.

    - Enhanced IRS enforcement aimed at high‑income noncompliance and complex business entities.
    - A continued limit on excess business losses for some pass‑through owners.
  - The nonpartisan Joint Committee on Taxation projected minimal average change for households under $400,000, with any small effects arising indirectly from how economists assign part of corporate taxes to workers and investors. Short answer: Congress does not prohibit the NIH from researching the causes of mass shootings. What federal law restricts is using NIH (and other HHS) funds to advocate or promote gun control, not to conduct scientific research.

Key facts
- The “Dickey Amendment” language, first applied to CDC funding in 1996 and later extended across HHS (including NIH), says appropriated funds “may not be used, in whole or in part, to advocate or promote gun control.” It does not ban research. NIH still includes this mandate in its grants policy. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11371))
- A 2019 Congressional Research Service brief explains that while CDC curtailed firearms work for years (in part after a 1997 budget reduction equal to what it had spent on firearm research), NIH told the Government Accountability Office it did not view the rider as preventing firearm‑related research. In 2018, Congress explicitly noted that CDC has authority to research the causes of gun violence notwithstanding the rider. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11371))
- In December 2019 (FY2020), Congress for the first time in decades appropriated dedicated federal funding—$25 million split between CDC and NIH—for firearm‑injury research; subsequent appropriations have continued NIH support. ([abcnews.go.com](https://abcnews.go.com/Health/congress-approves-unprecedented-25-million-gun-violence-research/story?id=67762555&utm_source=openai))

What this means today
- NIH can and does fund research on firearm injury and mortality prevention (which can include studying mass shootings and their risk factors), provided the work is scientific and not advocacy. The restriction is on advocacy, not on studying causes. ([grants.nih.gov](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section%204/4.2.3%20gun%20control.htm?utm_source=openai))

Why the misconception exists
- For many years, agencies—particularly CDC—reduced firearms research because the rider and related budget actions created a chilling effect, even though the statute itself targets advocacy. Congress and the executive branch have since clarified that research is allowed, and Congress has reestablished dedicated funding. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11371))

Confidence: high (based on NIH policy text, CRS analysis, and enacted appropriations).

He was never convicted of war crimes and, after denazification, worked for U.S. authorities. In the Cold War, West Germany rearmed and integrated into NATO; Heusinger helped build the new Bundeswehr, became its first Inspector General (1957–1961), and then served as Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee (1961–1964). NATO does not have a single “chief of staff”; the Military Committee’s chair is the Alliance’s senior military adviser, not a commander of NATO forces. ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))

Why this happened (with sources)
- His wartime role was professional staff work, not Hitler’s personal staff: Heusinger led the OKH Operationsabteilung (operations section) from 1940, placing him in the army’s senior planning circle and at regular Lage (situation) conferences with Hitler. He was injured in the 20 July 1944 explosion and then briefly held by the Gestapo. ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- Post‑war screening and U.S. use: After 1945 he was a U.S. prisoner of war, then served as a witness/expert for U.S. war‑crimes proceedings and worked in the U.S. Army Historical Division; in 1948 he became head of analysis in the CIA‑supervised Gehlen Organization. In denazification he was classified “affected, but not incriminated” (betroffen, aber nicht belastet). These factors made him employable in West German and Allied institutions. ([deutsche-biographie.de](https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/dbo067347.html?language=en))
- West German rearmament and integration into NATO: As Bonn decided to rearm within the Western alliance, Heusinger advised Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, took part in the 1950 Himmerod conference on building new forces, and rose to be the Bundeswehr’s first Inspector General (1957–1961). His experience and political reliability in the eyes of the West led to his selection as Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee (1961–1964). ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- What his NATO job actually was: NATO’s own record shows Heusinger chaired the Military Committee in Permanent Session (1961–1963) and then the Military Committee (1963–1964). Short answer
New York City sprays pesticides when its mosquito surveillance shows a heightened risk of West Nile virus to people. Spraying is one part of an integrated program that prioritizes eliminating standing water and larviciding; adulticide truck spraying is used selectively, at night, in areas with documented risk. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/wnv/2024/wnvplan2024.pdf))

What the City is using
- Adulticides: Anvil 10+10 (d‑phenothrin/sumithrin with piperonyl butoxide), Duet (pyrethroids), and Merus 3.0 (pyrethrins). Larvicides include bacterial products such as VectoBac (Bti) and VectoLex (Ls). These products are registered for public‑health mosquito control and are the formulations listed by NYC for the 2024–2025 seasons. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray-2024.page))

Why public‑health officials spray
- West Nile virus has been detected in NYC mosquitoes every year since 1999, and it can cause severe neurologic disease and death; there is no human vaccine. In 2025 the City recorded multiple neuroinvasive WNV cases. Spraying helps quickly reduce infectious adult mosquito populations when surveillance indicates elevated risk. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))

Is the spraying “unsafe”?
- According to NYC Health and the U.S. EPA, when these pesticides are applied as ultra‑low‑volume sprays according to their labels, they are not expected to pose significant health risks to the general population. NYC notes some sensitive people may experience short‑term eye, throat, or skin irritation and advises simple precautions (e.g., staying indoors during spraying, using recirculate on AC). ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))
- EPA’s human‑health reviews of commonly used mosquito adulticides (pyrethroids/pyrethrins, including sumithrin) conclude they can be used for public‑health mosquito control “without posing unreasonable risks” when label directions are followed; EPA has added mitigation measures to address ecological concerns such as spray drift and risks to aquatic organisms and pollinators. ([epa.gov](https://www.epa.gov/mosquitocontrol/permethrin-resmethrin-d-phenothrin-sumithrinr-synthetic-pyrethroids-mosquito?utm_source=openai))

How decisions are made and when spraying happens
- NYC’s Comprehensive Mosquito Surveillance and Control Plan specifies that adulticiding is triggered by data (positive mosquito pools, species, persistence, season, proximity to people). Applications are done in the evening or early morning to limit human and pollinator exposure, with public notice at least 24 hours in advance. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/wnv/2024/wnvplan2024.pdf))

If you’re concerned about exposure
- You can sign up for spray notifications, stay indoors during operations, and report standing water so the City can remove breeding sites—steps NYC Health explicitly recommends. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))

Bottom line
NYC sprays not because it seeks to expose residents to “unsafe” chemicals, but because surveillance shows a real, recurring risk from West Nile virus. The products used are EPA‑registered and, per NYC Health and EPA, are considered low risk when applied properly, though simple precautions are advised and ecological safeguards are required. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))
